source.version: arXiv:2406.07016v5 [cs.CL], 3 Jul 2025 (document dated July 4, 2025). The title differs from the search record title ('Delving into ChatGPT Usage in Academic Writing through Excess Vocabulary'), which is the earlier arXiv title.
source.title_on_document: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary

paper_design_summary: The authors analyze word frequencies in 15.1 million English-language PubMed abstracts from 2010 to 2024. They compare each word's observed 2024 frequency with a counterfactual extrapolated from 2021-2022 frequencies, identify 'excess words', and use sets of excess style words to estimate a lower bound on the share of 2024 abstracts processed with LLMs (at least 13.5 percent), overall and by field, country, journal, and inferred author gender. No people are assigned to AI, and no creativity, novelty, or diversity outcome is measured.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing was assigned. The study compares observed word frequencies in published abstracts across years with a counterfactual extrapolation from pre-LLM years.
assignment.quote: we study vocabulary changes in over 15 million biomedical abstracts from 2010–2024 indexed by PubMed, and show how the appearance of LLMs led to an abrupt increase in the frequency of certain style words.

participants.exclusions: Corpus filters, not people: complete English-language abstracts with length 250-4000 characters (24,814,136 abstracts); restricted to publication years 2010-2024 (15,103,888 abstracts); 3,514 errata, corrigenda, correction, or retraction notices erased; contaminating strings removed from 286,744 abstracts.
participants.who: No human participants. The corpus is published biomedical abstracts (authors of PubMed-indexed papers). Population code is nominal only.
participants.country: Multiple (first-author affiliation countries; 50 countries in subgroup analysis)
participants.quote: This resulted in 24 814 136 abstracts. We then only analyzed papers with publication years from 2010 to 2024, giving us 15 103 888 abstracts for analysis.

ai_tool.name_model: Not specified; LLMs such as ChatGPT in general (no specific tool studied)
ai_tool.how_used: Unobserved LLM use by authors when writing or editing abstracts, inferred from excess word frequencies.

task.description: Writing of biomedical paper abstracts (real publications); not a creative or ideation task as defined in the codebook.

data_and_code.data_url: https://github.com/berenslab/llm-excess-vocab (yearly word-occurrence matrix as csv.gz); original data at https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/download

eligibility.reason: Corpus study of PubMed abstracts with no human participants and no assignment of AI (p. 7, Section 4.1). Its outcome is excess word frequency used to bound the share of LLM-processed abstracts (p. 4, Section 2.2), which is a measure of how much AI text exists, not a creativity, novelty, or cross-author diversity outcome. The codebook (Section 3) lists such studies in the screening report and omits them from the dataset, so it does not qualify as observational context either. Criterion 2 is marked not_met because the study has no participants to count.

one_line_finding: Excess style-word frequencies in 15.1 million PubMed abstracts imply that at least 13.5 percent of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs (Delta = 0.135, average of Delta_rare = 0.136 and Delta_common = 0.134), ranging from below 5 percent to over 40 percent across subcorpora (pp. 4-5, Figure 5, Section 2.2-2.3, Discussion).
open_questions: The paper discusses LLM homogenization of scientific writing only in passing, citing other work ('LLM outputs less diverse and novel than human-written text', p. 6); it measures no diversity outcome itself. Confirm that the reviewer agrees it falls under 'measure how much AI text exists with no diversity outcome' rather than observational context.
notes: Outcomes list is empty because the paper reports no outcome scored for creativity, novelty, usefulness, or cross-author diversity; its outcomes are word-frequency ratios (r) and gaps (delta, Delta) and counts of excess words per year (Figures 1-5, S1-S7). Key printed numbers for the record: 26.7 K words analyzed with p > 10^-4 in 2023 and 2024 (p. 2); 454 excess words in 2024 vs up to 190 in 2021 (p. 3, Figure 3); 379 excess style words in 2024 (p. 3); 291 rare style words at T = 0.02 (p. 4, Figure S6); Delta_rare = 0.136, Delta_common = 0.134, Delta = 0.135 (p. 4, Figure 5a); Covid content-word set Delta = 0.069 (p. 4); subgroups such as computation papers from China Delta = 0.41 and Korea Sensors Delta = 0.34 (p. 5). The paper states it did not use LLMs to write or edit the manuscript (p. 7, Section 4.6). The markdown conversion matches the PDF version (v5, July 4, 2025).
